title: CELPIP General Listening — Practice Test 31
instructions: Listen to the audio for each part and answer the questions. Each audio plays once.

listeningScripts.title: Gym Membership Cancellation
listeningScripts.text: Member: Hi, I'd like to cancel my gym membership. Customer Service Rep: I'd be happy to help. Can I ask why you're looking to cancel? Member: I'm relocating to British Columbia for work and won't be using the facility anymore. Rep: I understand. Let me pull up your account. What's your membership number? Member: It's GYM-47823. I've been a member for eighteen months. Rep: Great. I see you're on our premium monthly plan at $89 per month. When are you planning to move? Member: Three weeks from now. Rep: Okay. I can process the cancellation effective immediately, or we can set it to end on your move date. Which works better? Member: I prefer the move date, so three weeks from today. Rep: Perfect. That would be June 24th. I'll note that in your file. You won't be charged for July. However, I do need to let you know that you're in the middle of a two-year contract. There is a $150 early termination fee. Member: That's not fair. I wasn't told about that when I signed up. Rep: I apologize for that. Let me see what I can do. Since you've been loyal for eighteen months, I can reduce that fee to $75. That's the best I can offer. Member: Okay, I'll accept that.

listeningScripts.title: Apartment Viewing Discussion
listeningScripts.text: Renter: I'm interested in this one-bedroom apartment. What are the lease terms? Landlord: It's a one-year lease. The rent is $1,200 per month, due on the first of each month. Renter: That seems reasonable. What utilities are included? Landlord: Water and heating are included, but you pay for electricity and internet. Renter: I see. What about parking? Landlord: There's one dedicated parking spot in the lot. It's included in the rent. Renter: Perfect. When would I be able to move in? Landlord: If we sign the lease today, you can move in on July 1st. Renter: Is that two weeks from now? Landlord: Yes, exactly two weeks. Do you have any pets? Renter: I have a cat. Is that okay? Landlord: Yes, cats are allowed. There's a one-time pet deposit of $150. Renter: Alright. Can I get a few days to think about it? Landlord: Sure, take until the end of the week. After that, I have other interested renters.

listeningScripts.title: Workplace Safety Training: Fire Procedures
listeningScripts.text: Good morning. This is your mandatory workplace fire safety training. Please listen carefully. In case of fire alarm, first, stay calm. Second, evacuate using the nearest exit. Do not use elevators under any circumstances. Stairs are located at both ends of each hallway. Third, move to the designated assembly point in the parking lot north of the building. Check in with your team leader. Fourth, do not re-enter the building until an authorized person announces it's safe. Fire drills occur quarterly on the first Friday of March, June, September, and December at 2 PM. During drills, the process is identical to a real emergency. Everyone must participate. If you cannot evacuate due to disability, proceed to a designated refuge area and use the emergency call button. These refuge areas are marked on building maps. Fire extinguishers are located every twenty-five meters along hallways and near kitchen areas. Only trained staff should operate extinguishers. If you're not trained, alert a supervisor. Report any fire hazards such as blocked exits or damaged equipment to maintenance immediately. Violations of fire safety procedures may result in disciplinary action. Contact Safety Services with any questions.

listeningScripts.title: Toronto Transit Strike Reaches Day Five
listeningScripts.text: Good evening. The Toronto Transit Commission strike has now entered its fifth day, affecting nearly two million commuters across the Greater Toronto Area. The TTC and the union representing over 10,000 workers remain at odds over wages and benefits. Union spokesperson Maria Chen says members are seeking a 4.25 percent pay increase over three years, citing inflation and cost-of-living pressures. The TTC counters that budget constraints limit them to 2.5 percent. Downtown businesses report a 30 percent drop in foot traffic since Monday. City Council has called for emergency mediation sessions to resume tomorrow morning. Meanwhile, the public is turning to carpooling, cycling, and GO Transit as alternatives. Some schools have adjusted schedules to accommodate parents unable to reach their children. Negotiations are expected to intensify as both sides face increasing pressure from the community.

listeningScripts.title: Small Business Loan Program Discussion
listeningScripts.text:
Bank Manager Chris: Our small business loan program has been quite successful this year. We've approved 285 loans totaling 42 million dollars to local entrepreneurs. However, we've noticed our default rate is slightly higher than industry average at about 4.2 percent. We're considering tightening our lending criteria to reduce risk.

Economic Development Officer Lisa: I would caution against tightening the criteria too much, Chris. These small loans are crucial for community development and job creation. Yes, a few borrowers struggle, but 95 percent of our loans are performing well. If we make the qualification requirements too strict, we'll only serve well-established businesses with existing collateral. That defeats the purpose of supporting new entrepreneurs who are taking real risks.

Business Owner Marcus: I completely agree with Lisa. When I started my restaurant five years ago, traditional banks wouldn't touch me because I didn't have significant assets or a ten-year track record. Your bank took a chance on me, and now my business employs 12 people. If your criteria were stricter, I wouldn't be here. I think what you should focus on is better support systems after lending, like mentorship programs and financial coaching.

Bank Manager Chris: Marcus, your success story is exactly what we want to see. But we do have a fiduciary responsibility to our depositors. Maybe Marcus is right—perhaps the answer isn't stricter lending, but better support after approval. We could partner with business development organizations to provide mentoring and financial management training.

listeningScripts.title: Digital Privacy in the Workplace
listeningScripts.text: I want to talk about something that concerns me deeply—workplace monitoring and digital privacy. Many companies today monitor their employees constantly: they track keystrokes, monitor websites visited, log bathroom breaks through card access, and even use AI to analyze email and chat conversations. The argument is usually that this improves productivity and security, but I think it's gone too far. Yes, employers have legitimate security concerns, but the level of surveillance we're accepting is unprecedented. When employees feel constantly watched, it creates anxiety and erodes trust. Studies show that excessive monitoring actually decreases productivity and morale. Workers spend time trying to appear productive rather than actually being productive. Moreover, there's a moral issue here. As an employee, you're a person, not a machine to be optimized. You deserve privacy and dignity at work. I'm not arguing against all monitoring—reasonable security measures are necessary. But there's a middle ground between trusting employees completely and treating them like suspects. Companies that have implemented less invasive monitoring policies actually report higher employee satisfaction and retention. So my position is this: employers should use targeted monitoring only where necessary for genuine security reasons, not blanket surveillance of everything everyone does. Trust and respect for employee privacy create better workplaces.
